chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from one of the two Imams (peace be upon him), who said:
I asked him about a man who performed *dhahir* (expiation of zihar) from his wife five times or more. He said: Ali (peace be upon him) said: Upon him, for each time, is an expiation.

key_terms.ظَاهَرَ: To perform Dhahir (a form of divorce-like declaration in Islamic law where a husband says to his wife, 'You are to me like the back of my mother'),
key_terms.عَلِيٌّ ع: Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him), often cited as one of the 'two Imams' in this specific chain context.
key_terms.كَفَّارَةٌ: Expiation (a ritual act or payment required to atone for a specific religious obligation or transgression),
key_terms.مَكَانَ: In place of / for each (indicating a one-to-one correspondence between the act and the penalty).

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on expiation for repeating Zihar multiple times with the same wife?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Istibsar* clarifies the jurisprudential principle that each distinct instance of *dhahir* with the same wife constitutes a separate obligation for expiation (*kaffarah*), rather than a single cumulative penalty. This ruling underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on individual accountability for each specific act of *dhahir*, ensuring that the spiritual and legal consequences are fully addressed for every occurrence. It serves as a foundational text for understanding the granularity of expiation requirements in family law.
